question: What is the @Bean annotation and when do you use it?
title: @Bean Annotation in Spring — Usage and Purpose
direct_answer: The at-Bean annotation is a method-level annotation used inside a at-Configuration class to explicitly register a bean with Spring. The method's return value becomes the bean instance. You use it when you can't annotate the class itself with at-Component, typically for third-party library classes like ObjectMapper or RestTemplate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of how to register beans when you don't control the source code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting at-Bean on a method outside a at-Configuration class, which won't work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give real-world examples: registering Jackson's ObjectMapper, Spring's RestTemplate, or a DataSource from HikariCP

sections.title: Explicit Bean Registration with @Bean
sections.content:
The **@Bean** annotation lets you manually register beans by writing factory methods. You place it on methods inside a **@Configuration** class, and the method's return value becomes a Spring-managed bean. This is essential when you need to configure **third-party classes** you can't modify—like Jackson's **ObjectMapper**, Spring's **RestTemplate**, or HikariCP's **DataSource**. You can't put @Component on ObjectMapper because you don't own that source code. Instead, you write a method that constructs and configures the object, then annotate it with @Bean. Spring calls your method once (for singleton scope) during startup and stores the returned instance. The method name becomes the bean name unless you specify @Bean(name="customName"). You can inject dependencies into the method parameters—Spring resolves them automatically.

This gives you full control over construction logic: conditional instantiation, complex initialization, or reading properties to configure the bean.

sections.title: @Bean at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Registers a bean|Method return is the bean|Method name is the bean name|Lives in @Configuration
blue|When to Use It|~Programmatic control|Third-party classes|Conditional creation|Custom wiring
emerald|vs @Component|~Two registration styles|@Bean is explicit, a method|@Component scans a class|@Bean when you cannot edit the class
violet|Lifecycle Hooks|~Optional callbacks|initMethod / destroyMethod|Singleton by default|Called by the container

sections.title: Registering Third-Party Beans with @Bean
When to Use @Bean vs @Component
sections.content:
Use **@Bean** when you don't control the class source code. You can't add @Service to ObjectMapper or RestTemplate—they're in external JARs. Write a @Bean method to instantiate and configure them. Also use @Bean when bean creation requires **complex logic**: reading environment variables, conditional instantiation based on profiles, or multi-step configuration. For example, creating a DataSource requires setting JDBC URL, username, password, and pool size—easier to do in a method than via annotations.

Use **@Component** (or @Service, @Repository) when you own the class and it has simple construction. Most of your business logic classes—OrderService, CustomerRepository—should use @Component. If you find yourself writing trivial @Bean methods that just return new MyService(), switch to @Component on the class itself. The rule: @Component for your code, @Bean for third-party or complex setup.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting @Bean outside @Configuration**: Freshers annotate a regular @Service class method with @Bean. Spring ignores it unless the class is @Configuration. The method won't be called and no bean is registered.
- **Calling @Bean methods directly**: Calling objectMapper() from another method in the same class. In a @Configuration class, Spring intercepts these calls and returns the singleton. But freshers sometimes manually call the method thinking they're creating a new instance, leading to confusion about singleton behavior.
- **Not returning the object**: Writing a @Bean method that returns void or null. Spring stores null as the bean instance, causing NullPointerException when injected. Always return the configured object.
- **Forgetting method parameters inject dependencies**: Writing complex constructor logic inside the method instead of accepting dependencies as parameters. Spring can inject beans into @Bean method parameters automatically.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@Bean**: method-level annotation in @Configuration classes to manually register beans
**Return value**: the object returned from the method becomes the bean instance
**Third-party classes**: primary use case is registering library classes you can't annotate
**Method name**: becomes the bean name unless overridden with @Bean(name="...")
**Method parameters**: Spring injects dependencies automatically into @Bean method parameters
**Complex initialization**: use @Bean when construction requires multi-step logic or property-based config
**@Configuration required**: @Bean only works inside a class annotated with @Configuration or @SpringBootApplication

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The at-Bean annotation is used to explicitly register a bean with Spring. You put it on a method inside a at-Configuration class, and whatever the method returns becomes a Spring-managed bean. You'd use this when you can't add at-Component to the class itself. The most common scenario is third-party libraries. For example, if you want Jackson's ObjectMapper as a bean, you can't open the Jackson source code and add at-Service to it. Instead, you write a method in your config class that creates and configures the ObjectMapper, then annotate the method with at-Bean. Spring calls that method during startup and stores the returned instance. Here's another real-world example: creating a RestTemplate bean. RestTemplate is from Spring's web module—you don't own the code. You'd write a at-Bean method that returns new RestTemplate, maybe customizing timeouts or interceptors. The method name becomes the bean name, so if your method is called restTemplate, you can inject it elsewhere with at-Autowired RestTemplate restTemplate. One mistake freshers make is putting at-Bean on a method in a regular at-Service class. That doesn't work—at-Bean only works in at-Configuration classes. Another mistake is not returning the object from the method. If your at-Bean method returns void, Spring stores null and you'll get NullPointerExceptions. You can also inject dependencies into the method parameters. Spring resolves them automatically, so you can write a at-Bean method that takes RestTemplate as a parameter and uses it to build a PaymentClient.

speakable_v2.hook: You can't add @Component to Jackson's ObjectMapper — @Bean is how you hand Spring a class you don't own.

beats.text: @Bean is a method-level annotation placed inside a @Configuration class. The method creates and returns the object you want Spring to manage. Spring registers the return value as a bean, using the method name as the default bean name. The method can accept parameters — Spring resolves and injects them from the context automatically.

@Component works only when you own the source code and can add annotations. But third-party classes like Jackson's ObjectMapper or a database connection pool don't have @Component on them. @Bean lets you write the creation code yourself and hand the result to Spring.

items: Basic: @Bean on a no-arg method — Spring calls it once and registers the return value.
Named: @Bean(name="myBean") overrides the default method-name-based name.
With parameters: Spring injects each parameter from the context before calling the method.
Combined with @Scope, @Primary, @Lazy, or @DependsOn for advanced lifecycle control.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, AppConfig is a @Configuration class with an objectMapper() method annotated @Bean. Inside, you call new ObjectMapper() and register the JavaTimeModule so Java 8 date types serialize correctly. Spring calls this method once and makes the configured ObjectMapper available for injection anywhere in the app. sharp edge: if you put @Bean in a class annotated only with @Component (not @Configuration), the CGLIB proxy is absent and calling one @Bean method from another will create a new instance each time — breaking singleton semantics.

items: @Bean must live in a class that Spring scans — if the @Configuration class is outside the component scan package, its beans won't be registered.
Avoid business logic inside @Bean methods — keep them as thin factory methods.

speakable_v2.cap: @Bean is your escape hatch for beans you can't annotate directly — use it in @Configuration to register any class as a Spring-managed bean.

question: What is bean naming in Spring and how do you set a custom bean name?
title: Spring Bean Naming Conventions
direct_answer: Spring beans are named to enable lookup and distinguish multiple beans of the same type. By default, @Component beans are named after the class with a lowercase first letter. @Bean methods use the method name. Set custom names with @Component value, @Bean name attribute, or @Qualifier on the bean definition.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of Spring's bean naming conventions and why names matter
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the default lowercase-first-letter convention or that you can have multiple beans of the same type distinguished by name
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you'd need custom names: when you have multiple beans of the same type and use @Qualifier to select which one to inject

sections.title: Why Spring Beans Need Names
sections.content:
Every bean in Spring's container has a **unique name** (also called a bean identifier) that Spring uses to manage it. When you have only one bean of a type, Spring can inject it by type alone. But when you have **multiple beans of the same type**—like two DataSource beans for different databases, or two RestTemplate beans with different timeouts—you need names to tell them apart. By default, **@Component** beans get a name that's the class name with the first letter lowercased: UserService becomes "userService". **@Bean** methods in @Configuration classes use the method name as the bean name. You can override these defaults to give more meaningful names, especially when the bean's purpose isn't obvious from the class name.

Think of it like contacts in your phone—if you have two people named John, you name them "John Work" and "John Gym" to tell them apart. Bean names do the same thing for Spring.

sections.title: Bean Naming at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Default Name|~If you set none|Class name, lower first letter|OrderService to orderService|@Bean uses method name
blue|Custom Names|~Override the default|@Component("myName")|@Bean("myName")|Or @Qualifier
emerald|Why Names Matter|~Disambiguation|Pick among many beans|Qualifier by name|XML / SpEL references
violet|Aliases|~Multiple names|@Bean(name={"a","b"})|All point to one bean|Handy for migration

sections.title: Setting Custom Bean Names
When Custom Bean Names Matter
sections.content: Use **custom bean names** when you have multiple beans of the same type and need to distinguish them. Scenario 1: **Multiple data sources**—you might have "primaryDatabase" and "analyticsDatabase" beans, both of type DataSource, and services inject the one they need using @Qualifier. Scenario 2: **Different configurations of the same tool**—like "fastRestTemplate" with 2-second timeout and "slowRestTemplate" with 30-second timeout for external APIs. Scenario 3: **Descriptive names for clarity**—naming a bean "paymentProcessor" instead of letting it default to "stripePaymentServiceImpl" makes configuration more readable. The rule: if someone reading your @Qualifier annotation needs to understand what makes this bean special, give it a clear custom name.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing the lowercase convention**: Freshers often look for a bean named "UserService" when Spring registered it as "userService"—the default name lowercases the first letter.
- **Forgetting that @Bean uses method name**: If your method is named `customerRepo()` but returns a CustomerRepository, the bean name is "customerRepo" not "customerRepository"—you must use that exact name in @Qualifier.
- **Using custom names everywhere**: Don't customize names unless you need to—if you only have one UserService bean, the default name works fine and changing it just adds confusion. Only customize when you have multiple beans of the same type or when the default name isn't clear enough.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Bean name**: unique identifier Spring uses to manage and retrieve beans from the application context
**Default for @Component**: class name with lowercase first letter—UserService becomes "userService"
**Default for @Bean**: method name in the @Configuration class becomes the bean name
**Custom names**: use @Component("customName") or @Bean(name = "customName") to override defaults
**@Qualifier**: annotation used at injection points to specify which bean to inject when multiple beans of the same type exist
**Multiple beans of same type**: require unique names so Spring and you can tell them apart
**Name lookup**: you can retrieve beans programmatically using applicationContext.getBean("beanName") with the bean's name

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Bean naming is how Spring identifies and manages beans in its container. Every bean has a unique name that you can use to look it up or specify which one to inject when there are multiple beans of the same type. By default, at-Component beans get named after their class with the first letter lowercased—so UserService becomes userService. For at-Bean methods in configuration classes, the method name becomes the bean name. You can override these defaults by passing a value to the annotation. For example, at-Service with the value orderSvc gives you a bean named orderSvc instead of the default. This matters most when you've got multiple beans of the same type. Say you have two DataSource beans—one for your main database and one for reporting. You'd give them custom names like primaryDatabase and reportsDatabase, then use at-Qualifier at injection points to specify which one you want. The common mistake is not realizing the default lowercase convention exists, or customizing names when you don't need to. If you only have one bean of a type, the default name works fine. Only use custom names when you're distinguishing multiple beans of the same type or when the default name isn't descriptive enough for your configuration.

seo.metaDescription: Learn Spring bean naming conventions, how default names are derived from class names, and how to set custom names with @Component and @Bean annotations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Spring names your beans for free — but when you have two beans of the same type, knowing those names is the only way to pick the right one.

beats.text: Every Spring bean has a name — a string identifier used to look it up and to match @Qualifier references. By default, @Component and its specializations derive the name from the class name with the first letter lowercased. @Bean methods use the method name. Custom names override the default by passing a string value to the annotation.

Bean names are how you resolve ambiguity. When you have two beans of the same type, type-based injection alone fails. @Qualifier uses the bean name to select the right one. Understanding names is also essential when using applicationContext.getBean() for dynamic lookup.

items: Default for @Service/@Component: class name with lowercase first letter — UserService becomes userService.
Default for @Bean method: method name — public DataSource primaryDataSource() becomes bean name primaryDataSource.
Custom single name: @Component("myBean") or @Bean(name="myBean").
Multiple aliases: @Bean(name={"primaryDs", "mainDs"}) — the bean answers to either name.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, there are two DataSource beans: devDataSource() and prodDataSource(). Their names are devDataSource and prodDataSource by default. You inject the right one with @Qualifier("devDataSource") at the injection point. gotcha: if you rename the method from devDataSource to devDs, the default name changes too — and any @Qualifier("devDataSource") references break silently. Use explicit @Bean(name="devDataSource") to lock the name.

items: Renaming a method that provides a @Bean changes the default bean name — existing @Qualifier references will break.
Two beans can't share the same name in the same context — Spring throws BeanDefinitionOverrideException unless you explicitly allow overriding.

speakable_v2.cap: Know the default naming rule, name your beans explicitly when they'll be referenced by @Qualifier, and never let a method rename silently change a bean name you depend on.

question: What is a bean definition in Spring?
title: Spring Bean Definition Explained
direct_answer: A bean definition is the metadata blueprint Spring uses to create and manage a bean. It contains the class type, scope (singleton or prototype), constructor arguments, property values, and lifecycle callbacks. Spring stores these definitions in the BeanFactory and instantiates objects from them when needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spring separates bean metadata (definition) from the actual object instance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking bean definition and bean instance are the same thing, when definition is the recipe and instance is the cooked meal
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Spring reads annotations or XML to create BeanDefinition objects before any beans are instantiated, showing you understand the two-phase process

sections.title: Bean Definition: The Blueprint Before the Object
sections.content:
A **bean definition** is Spring's internal recipe for creating a bean.

Think of it like a construction blueprint: the blueprint describes the house (class type, materials, dimensions), but it's not the house itself. When Spring starts up, it scans your code for **@Component**, **@Service**, **@Configuration** annotations and builds BeanDefinition objects containing all the metadata—class name, scope, dependencies, initialization methods. These definitions live in the **BeanFactory** registry. Later, when you need a bean, Spring reads the definition and constructs the actual object instance. This two-phase process (define, then instantiate) lets Spring analyze all dependencies upfront, detect circular references, and control the creation order. Without bean definitions, Spring would be just calling new OrderService() everywhere—no dependency injection, no lifecycle management, no singletons.

sections.title: Bean Definition at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Is|~A recipe, not the object|Class, scope, dependencies|Stored as a BeanDefinition|Metadata for the container
blue|How You Declare It|~Three ways|@Component plus scan|@Bean in @Configuration|XML (legacy)
emerald|What Is Inside|~The recipe details|Class name and scope|Constructor args|Init/destroy callbacks
violet|Who Reads It|~The IoC container|Reads definitions first|Then instantiates beans|Lazy or eager

sections.title: Registering and Inspecting Bean Definitions
When Bean Definitions Matter in Real Projects
sections.content: You directly interact with bean definitions when **customizing Spring's behavior**. In a multi-tenant application, you might programmatically register bean definitions at runtime using **BeanDefinitionRegistry** to create tenant-specific repositories. When building a plugin system, you read JAR files and register their beans dynamically. During **testing**, you use **@TestConfiguration** to override production bean definitions with mocks. Framework developers use **BeanFactoryPostProcessor** to modify definitions before any beans are created—for example, reading encrypted properties and injecting them into bean definitions. Most freshers won't write this code daily, but understanding the definition-versus-instance split helps debug why Spring can't find a bean or why a singleton isn't behaving as expected.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing definition with instance**: Freshers often think getBeanDefinition and getBean return the same thing. The definition is metadata; the instance is the living object. Modifying a definition after startup doesn't change existing singletons.
- **Expecting definitions to exist for manual new calls**: If you write new OrderService(gateway) instead of injecting it, Spring has no bean definition for that instance—it won't be managed, proxied, or eligible for @Transactional.
- **Not realizing definitions are created at startup**: All definitions are registered during application context refresh, before any bean is instantiated. If a class isn't scanned (wrong package) or lacks @Component, no definition exists and you'll get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **BeanDefinition**: metadata object containing class type, scope, dependencies, and lifecycle callbacks
**BeanFactory**: Spring container that stores definitions and creates bean instances from them
**Two-phase process**: Spring first registers all definitions, then instantiates beans in dependency order
**Scope in definition**: singleton vs prototype is stored in the definition, not decided per-request
**@Component family**: annotations trigger Spring to create a BeanDefinition for that class
**Programmatic registration**: use BeanDefinitionRegistry to add definitions at runtime
**Definition != instance**: changing a definition after context refresh doesn't affect existing singletons

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A bean definition is the metadata blueprint Spring uses to create a bean. It's not the bean itself—it's the recipe containing the class name, scope like singleton or prototype, constructor arguments, and lifecycle methods. When Spring starts, it scans your code for annotations like at-Service or at-Component and builds BeanDefinition objects. These live in the BeanFactory. Later, when you ask for a bean, Spring reads the definition and instantiates the actual object. Think of it like a cooking recipe versus the finished meal. The recipe describes ingredients and steps, but you can't eat it. You cook the meal from the recipe. Why does this matter? Because Spring analyzes all definitions upfront before creating any beans. That's how it detects circular dependencies and figures out the creation order. If you manually call new OrderService, there's no definition, so Spring can't inject dependencies or apply at-Transactional. One mistake freshers make is thinking the definition and instance are the same. They're not. The definition is created at startup; the instance is created when needed. For singleton scope, that's also at startup, but for prototype scope, a new instance is created every time you ask for the bean. Understanding this split helps you debug NoSuchBeanDefinitionException errors and know when Spring is managing your object versus when you're on your own.

seo.metaTitle: Spring Bean Definition Explained | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn what a Spring bean definition is, the metadata it contains, and the difference between a bean definition (blueprint) and a bean instance.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Spring reads your class like a blueprint before it ever builds the object — that blueprint is the bean definition.

beats.text: A bean definition is the metadata Spring stores to describe how to create a bean. It's not the bean itself — it's the recipe. It holds the class to instantiate, the scope (singleton or prototype), constructor arguments, properties to inject, and lifecycle method names. Spring reads all your annotations at startup and builds a registry of these definitions before creating any instances.

Separating the blueprint from the object lets Spring manage scope correctly. One definition can produce one singleton instance or hundreds of prototype instances depending on configuration. Without this separation, changing scope would require rewriting the creation logic.

items: Class: which Java class to instantiate — the core of the definition.
Scope: singleton means one shared instance; prototype means a new instance per injection.
Constructor arguments and properties: captured for dependency injection during instantiation.
Init and destroy method names: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy hook into the lifecycle.
Lazy flag: controls whether Spring creates the bean eagerly at startup or waits until first access.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, @Service on UserService causes Spring to register a bean definition: class=UserService, scope=singleton, constructor-arg=UserRepository. Later Spring uses that definition to create one UserService instance and inject it everywhere it's needed. candidates miss: there's always exactly one bean definition per registered bean, but singleton scope means one instance while prototype scope can produce many instances from that same definition.

items: Don't confuse the definition with the instance — asking how many bean definitions exist is different from asking how many bean instances are live.
Bean definitions are frozen after context refresh — you can't add new definitions at runtime in a standard Spring Boot app.

speakable_v2.cap: The bean definition is Spring's recipe card — one recipe, but the number of dishes it produces depends on the scope.

question: What is @Configuration in Spring and how is it different from @Component?
title: @Configuration vs @Component in Spring
direct_answer: at-Configuration marks a class as a bean definition source containing at-Bean methods. Spring CGLIB-proxies the class so calling a at-Bean method from another method returns the singleton instance, not a new object. at-Component just registers the class itself as a bean. at-Configuration is a specialized at-Component.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the CGLIB proxy behavior that enforces singleton semantics for at-Bean methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that at-Configuration creates a proxy to intercept at-Bean method calls and return the same singleton
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what happens if you call a at-Bean method directly from another at-Bean method in a at-Configuration class versus a plain at-Component class

sections.title: Why @Configuration Exists and How It Differs from @Component
sections.content:
Both **@Configuration** and **@Component** register a class as a Spring bean, but @Configuration has a special superpower: it's **CGLIB-proxied** to enforce singleton behavior for **@Bean** methods. When you call a @Bean method from another method in the same @Configuration class, Spring intercepts the call and returns the existing singleton instead of invoking the method again.

This prevents accidental duplicate bean creation.

Without this proxy, calling objectMapper() twice would create two ObjectMapper instances, breaking the singleton contract. @Component doesn't have this behavior—it's a simple bean registration. Use @Configuration when your class defines @Bean factory methods. Use @Component (or @Service, @Repository) when the class itself is the bean, not a factory for other beans. Technically, @Configuration is a specialized @Component (it's meta-annotated with @Component), so it's also component-scanned.

The difference is the proxy wrapping.

sections.title: @Configuration vs @Component
sections.content:
amber|@Configuration|~Defines @Bean methods|CGLIB-proxied class|Inter-bean calls return the singleton|The factory of beans
blue|@Component|~A scanned bean itself|No @Bean proxying|Just registers this class|A regular component
emerald|The Key Trap|~Inter-bean method calls|@Configuration caches the singleton|@Component makes a new object each call|The proxy is the difference
violet|When to Use|~Pick by intent|@Configuration for @Bean factories|@Component for services/utilities|Do not mix roles

sections.title: @Configuration vs @Component
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Configuration | @Component |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary purpose | Bean definition factory class | Register class itself as bean |
| CGLIB proxy | Yes, intercepts @Bean method calls | No proxy, direct instantiation |
| @Bean methods | Fully supported, singleton enforced | Ignored by Spring container |
| Inter-bean calls | Returns cached singleton | Calls method directly, new instance |
| Typical use case | Third-party bean registration | Business logic beans (services, repos) |

sections.title: @Component with @Bean methods - duplicates
@Configuration keeps singletons
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@Configuration** when your class contains **@Bean** methods to register other beans—especially third-party classes or beans needing complex setup. For example, an AppConfig class that creates ObjectMapper, DataSource, and RestTemplate beans. The CGLIB proxy ensures that if one @Bean method calls another @Bean method, you get the singleton, not a new instance.

Use **@Component** (or @Service, @Repository, @Controller) when the class itself is the bean. Your OrderService, CustomerRepository, PaymentController—these are business logic components. They don't produce other beans; they are the beans. If you accidentally use @Component on a class with @Bean methods, those methods are plain Java methods—Spring doesn't call them or register their return values. If one @Bean method calls another in a @Component class, you'll get multiple instances instead of singletons, causing subtle bugs like transaction managers being different across DAOs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Component for config classes**: Freshers write a config class with @Bean methods but annotate it with @Component instead of @Configuration. The @Bean methods aren't recognized, and no beans are registered. Even if Spring somehow processes them, calling one @Bean method from another creates a new instance every time instead of returning the singleton.
- **Not understanding the proxy**: Freshers call a @Bean method directly in a @Configuration class and wonder why their initialization logic runs once but they expected multiple times. The CGLIB proxy caches the result. If you want a new instance on every call, use prototype scope, not repeated method calls.
- **Overusing @Configuration**: Making every class @Configuration when it should be @Service. @Configuration is for factory classes, not business logic. Your OrderService shouldn't be @Configuration—it should be @Service.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@Configuration**: specialized @Component that marks a class as a bean definition factory
**CGLIB proxy**: Spring wraps @Configuration classes in a proxy to intercept @Bean method calls
**Singleton enforcement**: calling a @Bean method from another method returns the cached singleton
**@Component**: registers the class itself as a bean, no proxy, no @Bean method support
**Meta-annotation**: @Configuration is annotated with @Component, so it's component-scanned
**Inter-bean dependencies**: in @Configuration, method calls between @Bean methods are proxied
**Use @Configuration for**: third-party bean registration, complex initialization, factory classes

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: at-Configuration and at-Component both register a class as a Spring bean, but at-Configuration has a special behavior: Spring wraps it in a CGLIB proxy to enforce singleton semantics for at-Bean methods. Here's what that means. If you have a at-Configuration class with two at-Bean methods, and one calls the other, Spring intercepts that call and returns the existing singleton instead of running the method again. Without this proxy, you'd accidentally create multiple instances of the same bean. at-Component doesn't have this proxy—it's just a plain bean registration. If you put at-Component on a class and add at-Bean methods, Spring ignores those methods. They become regular Java methods, not bean factories. Let me give you a concrete example. Suppose you have a config class that creates an ObjectMapper bean and a PaymentClient bean. The PaymentClient needs the ObjectMapper. In a at-Configuration class, you'd write a paymentClient method that calls objectMapper to get the mapper. Spring intercepts that call and returns the singleton ObjectMapper bean. If you used at-Component instead, calling objectMapper would invoke the method directly, creating a new ObjectMapper every time. You'd end up with two ObjectMapper instances—one registered as a bean, another created by the direct method call. That breaks singleton scope. When should you use each? Use at-Configuration when your class is a factory for other beans—registering third-party classes, complex setup, multiple related beans. Use at-Component, or better yet at-Service or at-Repository, when the class itself is the bean. Your OrderService is at-Service, not at-Configuration. Your AppConfig class that creates ObjectMapper and RestTemplate beans is at-Configuration. The rule of thumb: if the class has at-Bean methods, use at-Configuration. If the class is the business logic, use at-Component or its specializations.

groups.heading: @Configuration
groups.text: Marks a class as a factory for @Bean definitions. Spring wraps it in a CGLIB proxy at startup. When any @Bean method is called — even directly from another @Bean method — the proxy intercepts and returns the existing singleton instead of creating a new object.

groups.heading: @Component
groups.text: Registers the class itself as a bean. No CGLIB proxy. If you put @Bean methods inside a @Component class, calling one @Bean method directly from another will bypass Spring and create a brand new object each time — breaking singletons.

items: Use @Configuration whenever you define @Bean methods — the proxy guarantee is essential for correct singleton behavior.
Use @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) when your @Bean methods are standalone and never call each other — it's faster to start up.
Use @Component for classes that don't define beans, like services, listeners, and utilities.

beats.text: gotcha: in our Spring Boot 3.2 AppConfig, beanA() calls beanC() directly. With @Configuration, Spring's proxy intercepts that call and returns the same C singleton that beanB() already received. Without the proxy (if you used @Component), A and B would each get a different C instance — subtle bugs with shared state.

speakable_v2.cap: @Configuration is @Component plus a proxy. Use @Configuration for bean factories; use @Component for everything else.

question: What is @Lazy in Spring and when would you use it?
title: @Lazy Bean Initialization in Spring
direct_answer: at-Lazy defers bean creation until the bean is first accessed. By default, singleton beans are created eagerly at application startup. Marking a bean or injection point with at-Lazy delays instantiation until it's actually needed. Useful for expensive beans or breaking circular dependencies, but delays error detection until runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring's eager versus lazy initialization strategies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overusing at-Lazy to speed up startup without understanding it hides errors that eager initialization would catch
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the trade-off: at-Lazy improves startup time but moves initialization errors from startup to runtime when the bean is first used

sections.title: Lazy Initialization: Speed vs Safety Trade-off
sections.content:
By default, Spring creates all **singleton** beans during application startup—this is called **eager initialization**. The container instantiates every @Service, @Repository, and @Configuration bean right away, even if they're not used immediately. **@Lazy** changes this behavior: it tells Spring to defer bean creation until the first time the bean is actually requested. You can put @Lazy on a bean class, a @Bean method, or an injection point (field, constructor parameter). The benefit is faster startup time—expensive beans like database connection pools or heavyweight third-party libraries don't block application startup. The downside is that initialization errors (missing dependencies, configuration mistakes, exceptions in constructors) are hidden until runtime when someone first accesses the bean.

In production, this can mean your app starts successfully but crashes on the first user request. @Lazy is also a trick to break **circular dependencies** where two beans reference each other—marking one injection point @Lazy delays its creation until after the dependency cycle is broken.

sections.title: @Lazy at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Delays bean creation|Not created at startup|Built on first use|Opposite of eager
blue|Default Behavior|~Singletons are eager|All built at boot|@Lazy flips this|Per-bean or per-config
emerald|When to Use|~Costly or rarely used|Heavy init beans|Can break some cycles|Faster startup
rose|Watch Out|~Hides errors|Config bugs surface late|Loses fail-fast safety|Use sparingly

sections.title: Step 1: Decide If Startup Time Is the Bottleneck
sections.content: First, measure your actual startup time and profile where it's spent. If your Spring Boot app starts in under 5 seconds, lazy initialization won't make a noticeable difference. If it's taking 30+ seconds because you have heavyweight beans—DataSource with connection pool preloading, Elasticsearch client with cluster health checks, large machine learning model loading—then @Lazy can help. Use @Lazy on those specific expensive beans, not everywhere. The key question: is the slow bean essential for the first request? If your app can't serve any request without the database, lazy-loading the DataSource just shifts the delay from startup to the first HTTP request. If the ML model is only needed for a specific admin feature, @Lazy makes sense—don't block startup for a feature 1% of requests use.

sections.title: Step 2: Understand the Error Detection Trade-off
sections.content: Eager initialization catches errors early—at startup, in your face, before production traffic hits. If you misspelled a @Value property, forgot to add a required dependency, or have a circular reference, you know immediately. @Lazy defers these errors. The app starts successfully, passes health checks, and deploys. Then the first user request tries to access the lazy bean, it fails to initialize, and you get a runtime exception. In cloud environments with auto-scaling, this can be catastrophic—new instances pass health checks but crash under load. Use @Lazy sparingly: only on beans where the startup cost is genuinely painful and the bean isn't used by every request. Never use @Lazy globally with spring.main.lazy-initialization=true in production unless you have comprehensive integration tests that touch every code path. That global flag hides all startup errors.

sections.title: Declaring and Injecting a @Lazy Bean
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Lazy everywhere to fix slow startup**: Freshers see a 15-second startup and annotate every bean with @Lazy. This masks the real problem (inefficient initialization logic) and moves errors to runtime. Fix the root cause instead—optimize database queries in @PostConstruct, remove unnecessary eager loading, or split heavyweight beans into separate modules.
- **Not understanding proxy behavior**: When you inject a @Lazy bean, Spring injects a proxy, not the real object. The first method call on that proxy triggers bean creation. Freshers sometimes serialize or reflect on the proxy and get confused by CGLIB classes in stack traces.
- **Using @Lazy to break circular dependencies without fixing the design**: Circular dependencies indicate poor design—two beans shouldn't depend on each other. @Lazy papers over the symptom but doesn't fix the coupling. Refactor one bean to use an event or callback instead of direct dependency.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@Lazy**: defers singleton bean creation until first access, improving startup time
**Default is eager**: Spring creates all singleton beans at startup by default
**Trade-off**: faster startup but errors move from startup to runtime when bean is used
**Lazy proxy**: Spring injects a proxy for @Lazy beans; first method call triggers instantiation
**Circular dependencies**: @Lazy on one injection point can break dependency cycles
**Global lazy**: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true makes all beans lazy (dangerous in production)
**Use case**: expensive beans not needed for every request (ML models, external clients)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: at-Lazy tells Spring to delay creating a bean until it's first used, instead of creating it at startup. By default, all singleton beans are created eagerly when the application starts. That's good because it catches errors early—if a bean can't be created, you know immediately. But it slows down startup. at-Lazy changes that. You put it on a bean class, a at-Bean method, or an injection point, and Spring skips creating that bean during startup. Instead, it injects a proxy. The first time you call a method on that proxy, Spring creates the real bean. When would you use this? Two main scenarios. First, when you have an expensive bean that's not needed right away. For example, a machine learning model that takes 10 seconds to load. If only 10% of your requests use that model, you don't want to block startup for everyone. Mark it at-Lazy, and it only loads when someone hits the ML feature. Second scenario is breaking circular dependencies. If BeanA needs BeanB and BeanB needs BeanA, Spring can't create either one first. Marking one injection point at-Lazy tells Spring to inject a proxy instead of the real bean, breaking the cycle. But here's the trade-off: at-Lazy hides errors. If that expensive bean has a configuration mistake, you won't find out at startup. Your app will start successfully, pass health checks, and deploy to production. Then the first user who triggers that bean gets an exception. So use at-Lazy carefully—only on specific beans where the benefit is worth the risk. Don't just slap at-Lazy everywhere to speed up startup. A common mistake freshers make is using at-Lazy to avoid fixing the real problem. If your startup is slow, profile it and optimize the heavyweight initialization logic—don't just hide it behind at-Lazy.

items: Eager (default): all singleton beans created at startup. Errors surface immediately. Startup is slower but predictable.

beats.text: Use @Lazy on a specific bean when it's genuinely expensive and not always needed — a report-generation service that's only called once a day, for example. Don't use it broadly in production. production trap: @Lazy on a misconfigured bean means the error doesn't appear until that bean is first requested — possibly hours into a production run.

items: You're adding @Lazy to fix a startup performance problem — profile first to confirm the bean is actually the bottleneck.
You're using @Lazy to work around a circular dependency — that's a workaround, not a fix. Refactor the design instead.

speakable_v2.cap: @Lazy is a targeted tool for genuinely expensive optional beans — don't sprinkle it everywhere hoping for a faster startup.

question: What is @DependsOn in Spring and when do you need it?
title: @DependsOn Bean Ordering in Spring
direct_answer: @DependsOn forces Spring to initialize specified beans before creating the annotated bean. It controls initialization order when there's no direct dependency that Spring can detect. Use it when one bean has a side effect—like schema creation or static resource setup—that another bean relies on, but there's no @Autowired field linking them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of explicit bean initialization ordering when implicit dependency wiring isn't enough
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @DependsOn when a proper @Autowired dependency would handle ordering automatically and more clearly
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @DependsOn is for initialization order, not runtime dependencies—the beans don't reference each other, but one must start first

sections.title: What @DependsOn Does and Why It Exists
sections.content:
Spring normally figures out bean initialization order by looking at **@Autowired** fields and constructor parameters. If bean A injects bean B, Spring knows to create B first. But sometimes bean X must start before bean Y even though Y doesn't inject X—maybe X creates database tables or initializes a cache that Y will use later. **@DependsOn** tells Spring "create these named beans before you create me" without requiring a direct reference.

Think of it like saying "this restaurant needs the power turned on before the ovens can start," even though the oven doesn't have a wire directly to the power plant. The **dependency is temporal** (one must happen first) not structural (one doesn't call the other). This annotation goes on the dependent bean—the one that needs to wait—and lists the names of beans that must be ready first.

sections.title: @DependsOn at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Forces init order|Create bean B before A|No direct dependency needed|An ordering hint
blue|When You Need It|~Hidden dependencies|Static init side-effects|Registration / setup beans|Not type-wired
emerald|How It Works|~Container reads it|Builds named beans first|Then the annotated bean|Reverse on shutdown
rose|Watch Out|~Smell if overused|Usually fix the design|Prefer explicit injection|String names are fragile

sections.title: Using @DependsOn for Initialization Order
When You Actually Need @DependsOn
sections.content: Use **@DependsOn** when bean A's initialization side effects are required before bean B starts, but B doesn't inject A. Common scenarios: (1) A **schema initializer** bean that creates tables before repository beans try to query them—the repository doesn't call the initializer, but needs its work done first. (2) A **cache warmer** that preloads data into a static cache before service beans start using it. (3) A **configuration bean** that writes files or sets system properties that other beans read during their construction. The key signal: you're getting errors during startup because something isn't ready yet, and adding @Autowired would be artificial since you don't actually need to call methods on the dependency.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @DependsOn instead of proper injection**: Freshers add @DependsOn when they should just @Autowired the dependency—if you actually call methods on the other bean, inject it normally and Spring handles order automatically.
- **Confusing initialization order with lazy loading**: @DependsOn doesn't delay your bean until runtime—it just controls which beans start first during application startup. Both beans still initialize eagerly.
- **Listing too many dependencies**: If you're depending on 5+ beans, you probably have a design problem—consider whether those should be injected dependencies or if your bean is doing too much at construction time.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@DependsOn**: forces Spring to create specified beans before the annotated bean, controlling initialization order
**Temporal dependency**: the dependency is about timing (one must start first), not code references (one doesn't call the other)
**Syntax**: @DependsOn("beanName") or @DependsOn({"bean1", "bean2"}) on the bean that needs to wait
**Default bean names**: @Component beans are named with lowercase-first-letter of class name unless you specify otherwise
**Not for runtime**: both beans still initialize at startup—@DependsOn doesn't lazy-load anything
**Prefer injection**: if you actually need to call methods on the other bean, use @Autowired—Spring handles order automatically
**Debug signal**: useful when you see startup errors about missing tables, uninitialized caches, or configuration not ready yet

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-DependsOn tells Spring to initialize certain beans before creating the annotated bean. It's for situations where one bean's startup side effects are needed by another, but there's no at-Autowired link between them. For example, imagine you've got a DatabaseSchemaInitializer bean that creates tables when it starts up, and an OrderService that queries those tables. The service doesn't inject the initializer—it doesn't call any methods on it—but it needs the tables to exist first. You'd put at-DependsOn on OrderService listing the initializer's bean name. Spring will then guarantee the initializer runs before the service starts. The key difference from normal injection is that this is about initialization order, not runtime dependencies. Both beans still start eagerly at application launch—at-DependsOn doesn't make anything lazy. The common mistake freshers make is using at-DependsOn when they should just inject the dependency normally. If you're actually calling methods on the other bean, inject it with at-Autowired and Spring handles the order for you. At-DependsOn is really for when the dependency is just about timing—one bean sets something up that the other will use later, but they don't directly interact.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @DependsOn is for the invisible dependency — when bean B needs bean A to have already run, but doesn't inject A directly.

beats.text: @DependsOn tells Spring to initialize a named bean before the annotated bean, even though there's no direct @Autowired link between them. It's purely an ordering guarantee. Spring normally determines initialization order from its dependency graph — @DependsOn extends that graph with an explicit edge for cases Spring can't infer automatically.

Spring can only detect order dependencies it can see — @Autowired fields and constructor parameters. Implicit side-effect dependencies, like 'bean A must run DDL before bean B reads the tables,' are invisible to Spring. @DependsOn makes them explicit.

items: Single dependency: @DependsOn("beanName") — ensures one named bean initializes first.
Multiple dependencies: @DependsOn({"beanA", "beanB"}) — both must initialize before the annotated bean.
Applicable to @Bean methods and @Component classes alike.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, DatabaseSchemaInitializer runs Flyway migrations at startup. CacheLoader reads from the freshly-migrated tables. CacheLoader doesn't inject DatabaseSchemaInitializer — it just needs the tables to exist. You add @DependsOn("databaseSchemaInitializer") on CacheLoader's @Bean method so Spring guarantees the migration completes first. non-obvious: if CacheLoader did @Autowire DatabaseSchemaInitializer, Spring would already order them correctly — @DependsOn is only needed when the link is invisible.

items: Don't use @DependsOn when a direct @Autowired dependency would do the job — the explicit injection is both cleaner and self-documenting.
Frequent use of @DependsOn is a design smell — it often means initialization logic should be consolidated into one bean.

speakable_v2.cap: @DependsOn is a last resort for side-effect ordering — if you can model the dependency explicitly with @Autowired, do that instead.
